newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam dong slips below 11,200 per dollar.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam dong slips below 11,200 per dollar.

text.p: The Vietnam dong slipped below 11,200 per U.S. dollar in muted interbank trade on Monday, settling at a new lower limit which was set by the central bank last week, dealers said.

In late afternoon the currency was quoted at 11,196/11,205 per dollar. The central bank has been managing a very gradual depreciation of the national currency for the past three months, nudging its official rate about 5-10 dong per dollar every week.
Authorised dealers in Vietnam's nascent interbank market may trade at rates of up to one percent on either side of the official rate, which was set at 11,094 per dollar on Saturday.
The latest official rate puts the dong's floor at 11,205 per dollar and its floor at 10,984.
Traders, noting that the dong had gone straight to its new floor on Monday, said demand for dollars remained very strong.

"We're trading right up there," said Peter McLean, Head of Treasury at Standard Chartered in Hanoi. "The market is not liquid with dollars at this point of time and so there is still excess demand in the market for dollars."
He forecast a four- to five-percent decline in the dong this year, which would take it to around 11,600 per dollar.
However, a foreign bank Treasury dealer in Ho Chi Minh City said he saw the central bank allowing an even bigger depreciation, to around 12,000 per dollar by year-end.

McLean said he saw little ahead to change the dong's downward trend, except the possibility of a big pick-up in foreign direct investment or a surge in remittances following the government's decision to scrap a five-percent tax on money sent from overseas.
Strong FDI flows and remittances from abroad helped underpin the dong 1994, 1995 and early 1996, when it was stable at around 11,000 per dollar.

Analysts say Vietnam, alarmed by a near-doubling of the trade deficit to $4.0 billion in 1996, is hoping its gradual depreciation policy will put a brake on imports and make the country's exports sell better.
